answer:
**לפי מנהג אשכנז אין שום דרך לטבול כעבור 10 ימים מהראייה. אצל ספרדים זה אפשרי מבחינה עקרונית, אבל לא בדרך שהצעת.** אי אפשר לספור שישה נקיים במקום שבעה, ואני לא מכיר קולא כזו בשם הבן איש חי. האפשרות היחידה קיימת לפי לשון השולחן ערוך (המחבר): ההמתנה לפני ההפסק נובעת רק מחשש "פולטת שכבת זרע" ונמדדת מזמן התשמיש, לא מזמן הראייה. לכן אשה ספרדייה שלא הייתה עם בעלה בימים שלפני הראייה, ושהדימום שלה קצר מאוד, יכולה תיאורטית לטבול בערך בליל היום העשירי.

## עיקרי הדברים
- **שבעה נקיים הם חובה מוחלטת.** זו חומרת בנות ישראל שהתקבלה בכל הקהילות, ואין דעה מקובלת שמסתפקת בשישה.
- **"4 ימים" של הרב עובדיה הם ההמתנה כשהייתה תשמיש סמוך לראייה.** גם לפיהם, הטבילה המוקדמת ביותר היא בליל היום ה-12.
- **לפי המחבר, אם לא היה תשמיש ב-6 העונות (כ-3 ימים) שלפני ההפסק, אין חובה להמתין בכלל.** אפשר לעשות הפסק טהרה ברגע שהדימום פוסק.
- **הרמ"א (אשכנזים, וגם חב"ד) מחייב תמיד 5 ימים, גם בלי תשמיש וגם על כתם,** וכותב "ואין לשנות". לכן הטבילה המוקדמת ביותר היא בליל היום ה-13.

## 1. שבעה נקיים: אין מקום לספור שישה
מן התורה, נדה טמאה שבעה ימים מהראייה. אבל בנות ישראל החמירו לספור שבעה ימים נקיים אחרי שהדם פוסק (חומרת ר' זירא, [Niddah 66a]). הרמב"ם והשולחן ערוך פסקו כך, וזה נוהג בכל הקהילות בלי יוצא מן הכלל.

לא הצלחתי לאתר בבן איש חי (או בשום מקור אחר) היתר לספור שישה נקיים, ולפי מה שאני יודע אין דבר כזה. ייתכן שמדובר בבלבול עם אחת מההלכות האלה:
- **בדיעבד מספיקות שתי בדיקות.** אם האשה בדקה רק ביום הראשון וביום השביעי, הספירה כשרה. זו קולא לגבי הבדיקות, לא לגבי מספר הימים.
- **"מקצת היום ככולו".** זה עניין אחר לגמרי. היום השביעי צריך להסתיים לפני הטבילה, ואסור לטבול ביום השביעי לפני צאת הכוכבים.

אם יש לך מקור מדויק בבן איש חי, אשמח לעיין בו יחד איתך. בכל מקרה, אסור לסמוך על זה הלכה למעשה.

## 2. מאיפה מגיעים "4 הימים": לשון המחבר
וזה לשון המחבר:
> "המשמשת מטתה וראתה אחר כך ופסקה אינה מתחלת לספור ז' נקיים עד שיעברו עליה ו' עונות שלימות שמא תפלוט... כגון אם שמשה במוצאי שבת אינה מתחלת לספור עד יום ה'" [Shulchan Arukh, Yoreh De'ah 196:11]

הרמ"א מוסיף שם: "ותפסוק יום ד' לעת ערב ויום ה' עולה למנין".

מכאן שלוש נקודות חשובות:
- **הטעם הוא רק חשש פליטת זרע.** ההמתנה נקבעת לפי זמן התשמיש, לא לפי זמן הראייה.
- **"4 ימים" זה המקרה הרגיל של תשמיש ממש לפני הראייה.** תשמיש במוצאי שבת, הפסק ביום רביעי לפני השקיעה, וחמישי הוא היום הראשון לספירה.
- **אם לא היה תשמיש בתוך 6 העונות, אין לפי המחבר שום שיעור המתנה.** זה כולל גם מקרה שהתשמיש היה כמה ימים לפני הראייה ו-6 העונות כבר עברו. האשה עושה הפסק ברגע שהדם פוסק. ידוע לי שזו גם הכרעת הרב עובדיה יוסף בספרו "טהרת הבית", אבל לא הצלחתי לבדוק את לשונו עכשיו, ולכן כדאי לוודא.

## 3. החשבון בפועל (יום הראייה הוא יום 1)

| מקרה | הפסק טהרה | שבעה נקיים | הטבילה המוקדמת ביותר |
|---|---|---|---|
| **ספרדיה, תשמיש סמוך לראייה** (4 ימים) | יום 4 לפני השקיעה | ימים 5–11 | ליל יום 12 |
| **ספרדיה, בלי תשמיש בתוך 6 עונות, דימום שפסק ביום 2** | יום 2 | ימים 3–9 | **ליל יום 10** |
| **ספרדיה, בלי תשמיש, דימום שפסק ביום 1** (נדיר מאוד) | יום 1 | ימים 2–8 | ליל יום 9 |
| **אשכנזיה / חב"ד** | יום 5 לפני השקיעה | ימים 6–12 | ליל יום 13 |

כלומר, התשובה לשאלה היא **כן, אבל רק בשורה השנייה**: אשה ספרדייה, בלי תשמיש בימים שלפני ההפסק, ושהדם שלה פסק כבר ביום השני. זה יכול לקרות למשל אצל כלה לפני החתונה, כשהבעל היה בנסיעה, או אצל אשה שלא שימשה מסיבה אחרת. במחזור רגיל, שבו הדימום נמשך 4–6 ימים, השאלה לא רלוונטית בכלל: ההפסק אפשרי רק אחרי שהדם פוסק בפועל.

הצירוף שהצעת (4 ימים ועוד 6 נקיים) אינו מבוסס, כי חציו השני לא קיים.

## 4. אשכנזים
הרמ"א מביא שנהגו להמתין יום נוסף מחשש טעות בבין השמשות. לאחר מכן הוא פוסק: "שעכשיו אין לחלק בין שמשה עם בעלה ללא שמשה וכל אשה שרואה אפי' כתם צריכה להמתין ה' ימים עם יום שראתה בו... וכן נוהגין במדינות אלו ואין לשנות" [Shulchan Arukh, Yoreh De'ah 196:11]. לכן אצל אשכנזיות (וכך גם בחב"ד) אין מצב שהטבילה תהיה לפני ליל היום ה-13.

## 5. עוד שתי נקודות
- **שעת הטבילה:** טובלים רק בלילה שאחרי היום השביעי, ולא ביום השביעי עצמו. גם "לטבול ביום העשירי" במובן של שעות היום אסור.
- **בעיות פוריות:** לפעמים השאלה עולה כי הביוץ מוקדם, והטבילה הרגילה מגיעה אחריו. במקרה כזה כדאי מאוד לפנות לרב מומחה בטהרת המשפחה, ולעיתים גם לגורם רפואי שמכיר את ההלכה (למשל מכון פוע"ה). יש פתרונות מוכרים, אבל צריך לבדוק כל מקרה לגופו.

**חשוב:** בהלכות נדה כל פרט משנה: מתי בדיוק היה התשמיש, מתי פסק הדם, ומה המנהג שלך. זו שאלה שחייבת להגיע לרב שיכול לשאול שאלות המשך. אל תסמכי על החשבון שכאן בלי לבדוק איתו. כדאי להתייעץ עם רב לגבי המקרה שלך.

answer:
Die Tora verbietet nicht, den Bart zu schneiden. Sie verbietet, ihn mit einem Rasiermesser zu „zerstören“, also an der Wurzel abzurasieren ([Leviticus 19:27]). Bartschneiden oder Stutzen mit der Schere ist nach der Halacha ausdrücklich erlaubt ([Shulchan Arukh, Yoreh De'ah 181:10]). Dass viele fromme Juden ihren Bart gar nicht schneiden, geht auf eine zusätzliche Strenge und vor allem auf kabbalistische Gründe zurück. Es ist kein allgemeines Tora-Verbot.

## Das Wichtigste in Kürze
- Das Verbot: Ein Mann darf die fünf „Ecken“ (*Pe'ot*) seines Bartes nicht mit einem Rasiermesser (*Ta'ar*) rasieren.
- Mit der Schere ist das Schneiden erlaubt, nach dem Mechaber sogar ganz kurz. Der Rema rät nur zu einer bestimmten Vorsicht beim Schneiden.
- Weil die Gelehrten uneinig sind, wo genau die fünf Ecken liegen, soll ein *Jerej Schamajim* (Gottesfürchtiger) laut Shulchan Arukh nirgends am Bart ein Rasiermesser benutzen.
- Den Bart überhaupt nicht zu schneiden, ist ein kabbalistischer Brauch. Er stammt vor allem aus dem Sohar und vom Arizal und wird unter Chassidim und in Chabad besonders gepflegt.
- Zu bestimmten Zeiten schneidet man sich nach Brauch den Bart nicht: in der Omerzeit, in den Drei Wochen, an Chol HaMoed und in der Trauerzeit.

## 1. Der Tora-Vers
> „לֹא תַקִּפוּ פְּאַת רֹאשְׁכֶם וְלֹא תַשְׁחִית אֵת פְּאַת זְקָנֶךָ“
> „Ihr sollt die Ecke eures Kopfes nicht rund scheren, und du sollst die Ecke deines Bartes nicht zerstören.“ [Leviticus 19:27] (meine Übersetzung)

Bei den Kohanim (Priestern) wird das Verbot noch einmal wiederholt (Lev. 21:5): „Die Ecke ihres Bartes sollen sie nicht scheren.“

## 2. Was genau verboten ist: der Talmud
Der Talmud ([Makkot 21a]) leitet aus den beiden Ausdrücken „scheren“ (*Giluach*) und „zerstören“ (*Haschchata*) Folgendes ab:
- Verboten ist nur ein Scheren, das zugleich zerstört, also das Haar an der Wurzel entfernt. Das ist das **Rasiermesser**.
- Die **Schere** schneidet zwar, zerstört aber nicht. Daher ist man damit nicht strafbar.
- Pinzette oder Hobel zerstören zwar, sind aber kein „Scheren“, und auch dafür ist man nicht strafbar. Rabbi Eliezer ist bei diesen anderer Meinung, die Halacha folgt aber den Rabbanan.
- Es gibt **fünf Ecken**: „zwei von hier, zwei von dort und eine von unten“.

## 3. Der Grund für das Verbot
Der Rambam erklärt es so: **Götzenpriester pflegten ihren Bart abzurasieren.** Deshalb hat die Tora das Abrasieren verboten, damit sich Israel von ihnen unterscheidet ([Mishneh Torah, Foreign Worship and Customs of the Nations 12:7]). Er zählt die fünf Ecken auf: den oberen und unteren Wangenbereich rechts, dasselbe links, und das Kinn. Für jede Ecke ist man einzeln strafbar. Er schließt daraus ausdrücklich: „Wer seinen Bart mit der Schere geschoren hat, ist frei.“

Der Rambam erwähnt noch etwas: Den Schnurrbart darf man sogar mit dem Rasiermesser rasieren. Trotzdem hat sich in Israel der Brauch durchgesetzt, ihn nur zu stutzen, damit er beim Essen und Trinken nicht stört ([Mishneh Torah, Foreign Worship and Customs of the Nations 12:8]).

## 4. Die Halacha: Mechaber und Rema
Im Shulchan Arukh [Shulchan Arukh, Yoreh De'ah 181:10–11] steht Folgendes:
- **Mechaber, gültig für Sefarden:** „אבל במספרים מותר אפילו כעין תער“, das heißt: Mit der Schere ist es erlaubt, selbst so kurz wie mit einem Rasiermesser.
- **Rema (Glosse, gültig für Aschkenasen):** Man soll trotzdem vorsichtig sein. Beim Schneiden mit der Schere soll man mit dem oberen Blatt arbeiten und nicht nur mit dem unteren an der Haut entlangfahren. Sonst wirkt die Schere wie ein Rasiermesser. Unter dem Hals sei dies weniger kritisch.
- **Mechaber (11):** Die Gelehrten sind sich über die Lage der fünf Ecken uneinig. „לפיכך ירא שמים יצא את כולם ולא יעביר תער על כל זקנו כלל“, das heißt: Deshalb soll ein Gottesfürchtiger alle Meinungen erfüllen und überhaupt kein Rasiermesser an seinen Bart bringen. Der Rema fügt hinzu: auch nicht unter dem Hals.

**Fazit nach der Halacha:** Ein Rasiermesser oder ein Nassrasierer am Bart ist verboten. Die Schere und ein Bartschneider (Trimmer) sind erlaubt.

### Elektrorasierer
Ob Elektrorasierer erlaubt sind, ist unter heutigen Poskim umstritten (das gebe ich hier aus dem Gedächtnis wieder):
- Der Chafez Chaim war streng und verbot sie.
- Viele Poskim, etwa Rav Moshe Feinstein und für Sefarden Rav Ovadia Yosef, erlauben Geräte, die wie eine Schere schneiden: Eine Klinge hinter einem Sieb schneidet das Haar.
- Bei Modellen mit sogenanntem „Lift-and-Cut“-System, die das Haar anheben und tiefer abschneiden, sind viele vorsichtig oder verbieten sie.

Hier ist es wichtig, beim eigenen Rabbiner nachzufragen, welches Gerät er erlaubt.

## 5. Warum viele den Bart gar nicht schneiden: der Sod (die kabbalistische Ebene)
Diese Ebene ist der eigentliche Hintergrund deiner Frage:
- **Sohar:** Die Idra Rabba im Sohar beschreibt die Haare des „himmlischen Bartes“ (*Dikna*) als Kanäle der göttlichen Barmherzigkeit. Seine 13 „Tikkunim“ (Anordnungen) entsprechen den 13 Eigenschaften der Barmherzigkeit (*Jud-Gimmel Middot*). Der menschliche Bart gilt als Abbild davon. Deshalb soll man nicht einmal ein einziges Haar entfernen.
- **Arizal:** Nach Rabbi Chaim Vital nahm der Arizal überhaupt keine Haare aus seinem Bart, auch nicht mit der Schere.
- **Chassidut und Chabad:** Unter Chassidim ist der volle, ungeschnittene Bart weit verbreitet. Der Zemach Zedek (der dritte Lubawitscher Rebbe) hat sehr scharf gegen das Abschneiden des Bartes geschrieben, und der Lubawitscher Rebbe hat dies stark betont. In Chabad gilt der ungeschnittene Bart deshalb als selbstverständlich.

Diese Gründe sind **Brauch und Frömmigkeit** (*Minhag* bzw. *Hiddur*), keine verbindliche Halacha für alle. Viele toratreue Aschkenasen und Sefarden stutzen ihren Bart mit der Schere oder benutzen einen erlaubten Elektrorasierer. Das ist halachisch völlig legitim.

## 6. Zeiten, in denen man sich nicht rasiert
Unabhängig vom Grundverbot schneiden sich Juden nach Brauch zu bestimmten Zeiten weder Bart noch Haare:
- in der Omerzeit, je nach Gemeinde in unterschiedlichen Abschnitten,
- in den Drei Wochen (17. Tammus bis 9. Aw), bei Sefarden meist nur in der Woche des 9. Aw,
- an Chol HaMoed,
- in der Trauerzeit (*Schloschim*, für Eltern länger).

## Zusammengefasst nach Gemeinde
- **Aschkenasisch:** Kein Rasiermesser. Die Schere ist erlaubt, mit der Vorsicht des Rema. Viele benutzen einen vom Rabbiner erlaubten Elektrorasierer.
- **Sefardisch:** Kein Rasiermesser, nirgends am Bart. Die Schere ist erlaubt, auch sehr kurz. Viele Sefarden lassen aus kabbalistischen Gründen den Bart ganz wachsen.
- **Chabad und Chassidim:** Der Bart wird in der Regel überhaupt nicht geschnitten.

Für deinen persönlichen Fall, etwa welches Rasiergerät du benutzen darfst oder welchem Brauch du folgen sollst, wende dich bitte an deinen Rabbiner.

answer:
**Respuesta corta:** sí, en parte, pero solo en Estados Unidos y Canadá, y solo para ir a la sinagoga. En 1950, el Comité de Ley y Normas Judías (CJLS) de la Asamblea Rabínica conservadora aprobó una decisión llamada *A Responsum on the Sabbath*. Permite ir en coche a los servicios de Shabat a quien vive demasiado lejos para ir caminando. No permite viajar por otros motivos. El movimiento Masorti de Israel nunca aceptó esa decisión: allí conducir en Shabat sigue prohibido. Según la halajá tradicional (ortodoxa), conducir en Shabat está prohibido tanto para asquenazíes como para sefardíes.

## Puntos clave
- La Torá prohíbe encender fuego en Shabat [Exodus 35:3], y "encender" (*mav'ir*) es uno de los 39 trabajos prohibidos [Mishnah Shabbat 7:2]. El motor de un coche quema combustible.
- La decisión conservadora de 1950 es una excepción limitada: solo vale para ir a rezar con la comunidad. No cubre paseos, compras ni visitas.
- El Masorti israelí y muchos rabinos y fieles conservadores observantes no la siguen y van caminando.
- Las autoridades ortodoxas, asquenazíes y sefardíes por igual, prohíben conducir en Shabat. En caso de peligro para la vida (*pikuaj néfesh*), todos lo permiten.

---

## 1. La base tradicional de la prohibición

- **Encender fuego:** dice la Torá: "לֹא־תְבַעֲרוּ אֵשׁ בְּכֹל מֹשְׁבֹתֵיכֶם בְּיוֹם הַשַּׁבָּת" ("No encenderéis fuego en ninguna de vuestras moradas el día de Shabat") [Exodus 35:3]. La Mishná incluye *hamav'ir* (encender) y *hamejabé* (apagar) entre los 39 trabajos principales [Mishnah Shabbat 7:2]. Para los poskim ortodoxos, la combustión del motor cae dentro de esta prohibición. Además entran en juego el uso de la electricidad del vehículo y, a menudo, el transporte de objetos fuera de un *eruv*.
- **Límite de distancia (*tjum Shabat*):** "שְׁבוּ אִישׁ תַּחְתָּיו אַל־יֵצֵא אִישׁ מִמְּקֹמוֹ בַּיּוֹם הַשְּׁבִיעִי" ("Quédese cada uno en su lugar; que nadie salga de su lugar el día séptimo") [Exodus 16:29]. De este versículo los sabios derivan el límite de 2000 *amot* fuera de la ciudad, que regula el Shulján Aruj en las leyes de *tjum* (Oraj Jaim, a partir del siman 397).
- **Montar:** los sabios prohibieron montar a caballo en Shabat, como medida rabínica (*shevut*) (Mishná Beitzá, cap. 5). Por eso los viajes en vehículo eran ajenos al Shabat tradicional incluso antes de existir el motor.

**Práctica ortodoxa:** no hay diferencia entre asquenazíes (Rema y Mishná Berurá), sefardíes (Shulján Aruj y Rav Ovadia Yosef) y Jabad: conducir en Shabat está prohibido. Ir como pasajero tampoco está permitido, aunque conduzca un no judío, por las leyes de *tjum*, la prohibición de pedir a un no judío que trabaje por uno (*amirá le-nojrí*) y otras razones.

## 2. La postura conservadora: la decisión de 1950

En 1950 el CJLS adoptó una decisión escrita por los rabinos Morris Adler, Jacob Agus y Theodore Friedman. Sus argumentos centrales fueron estos:

- **Contexto:** tras la Segunda Guerra Mundial, muchas familias judías de EE. UU. se mudaron a los suburbios, lejos de las sinagogas. Los autores temían que, si no podían asistir, la gente dejara por completo la vida comunitaria de Shabat.
- **Razonamiento:** trataron la oración comunitaria como un valor capaz de justificar una *takaná* (enmienda legal) para su época. Además, sostuvieron que la combustión dentro del motor no equivale al encendido de fuego que prohíbe la Torá.
- **Límites:** el permiso cubre **solo** el viaje de ida y vuelta a los servicios. No se extiende a paseos, compras, trabajo ni visitas sociales. En esa misma decisión también se permitió encender luces eléctricas en Shabat.

**Matices importantes:**
- Dentro del movimiento conservador nunca hubo consenso. El CJLS suele aprobar varias opiniones como válidas, y cada rabino local (*mará de-atra*) decide para su comunidad. Muchos rabinos conservadores animan a vivir cerca de la sinagoga y a caminar, y lo hacen ellos mismos.
- Con los años, varias voces del movimiento consideraron que el permiso tuvo efectos no deseados. Por ejemplo, se pasó de "conducir a la sinagoga" a "conducir en general". No pude verificar ahora el texto de esas evaluaciones posteriores, así que no las cito en detalle.

## 3. El movimiento Masorti en Israel y en otros países

- **Israel:** la Asamblea Rabínica de Israel y su comité de halajá (*Va'ad Halajá*) no adoptaron la decisión de 1950. Allí las comunidades están a poca distancia a pie, así que desaparece la razón principal del permiso. En el Masorti israelí, conducir en Shabat no está permitido.
- **América Latina:** en las comunidades vinculadas al Seminario Rabínico Latinoamericano, la práctica varía según la comunidad y su rabino. Si usted pertenece a una de ellas, conviene preguntar directamente cuál es su norma.

## 4. Peligro para la vida

En una emergencia médica o ante cualquier peligro para la vida (*pikuaj néfesh*), todas las corrientes coinciden: hay que conducir o llamar a una ambulancia sin dudarlo. Salvar una vida tiene prioridad sobre el Shabat.

---

**Nota sobre las fuentes:** pude consultar directamente los versículos y la Mishná citados. No pude consultar en este momento los textos del Shulján Aruj sobre *tjum* ni el de la Mishná Beitzá, por eso los menciono sin número exacto o solo por capítulo. La decisión conservadora de 1950 no está en Sefaria; la describo a partir de mi conocimiento general.

Para su situación concreta, consulte a su rabino. Si es de una comunidad masortí, su propio rabino es quien fija la norma local.

answer:
Sim, em certo sentido. Um gentio não tem a obrigação de sentar na *sucá* (cabana de Sucot), porque a Torá dirige o mandamento a Israel. Mas, segundo o Rambam, se ele quiser cumprir uma mitsvá da Torá para receber recompensa, e a fizer corretamente, não o impedimos. O Talmud ensina que ele recebe recompensa, embora menor do que a de quem tem a obrigação.

## Pontos principais
- **Não é obrigatório:** o versículo limita o dever "a todo cidadão em Israel" [Leviticus 23:42].
- **É permitido:** um *ben Nôach* (gentio que guarda as leis dadas a Noé) que queira cumprir uma mitsvá da Torá pode fazê-lo [Mishneh Torah, Kings and Wars 10:10].
- **Há recompensa:** ele é recompensado "como quem não foi ordenado e cumpre", o que é menos do que quem foi ordenado [Avodah Zarah 3a].
- **Sucot e as nações:** o Talmud escolhe justamente a sucá como a mitsvá que, no futuro, será oferecida às nações como teste.

## 1. A fonte: a obrigação é de Israel
A Torá diz:
> בַּסֻּכֹּת תֵּשְׁבוּ שִׁבְעַת יָמִים כׇּל־הָאֶזְרָח בְּיִשְׂרָאֵל יֵשְׁבוּ בַּסֻּכֹּת
> "Nas cabanas habitareis sete dias; todo cidadão em Israel habitará em cabanas." [Leviticus 23:42]

A expressão "em Israel" mostra que o mandamento cabe ao povo judeu. Os gentios estão obrigados apenas às sete leis de Noé.

## 2. A halachá: um gentio pode cumprir a mitsvá voluntariamente
O Rambam escreve:
> בֶּן נֹחַ שֶׁרָצָה לַעֲשׂוֹת מִצְוָה מִשְּׁאָר מִצְוֹת הַתּוֹרָה כְּדֵי לְקַבֵּל שָׂכָר, אֵין מוֹנְעִין אוֹתוֹ לַעֲשׂוֹתָהּ כְּהִלְכָתָהּ
> "Um *ben Nôach* que deseja cumprir uma das outras mitsvot da Torá para receber recompensa: não o impedimos de cumpri-la corretamente." [Mishneh Torah, Kings and Wars 10:10] (tradução minha)

Ele fala de um *ben Nôach*, ou seja, de quem já guarda as sete leis. A palavra כְּהִלְכָתָהּ ("corretamente") indica que, se ele quiser sentar numa sucá, ela deve ser uma sucá válida. Na mesma parte da obra, o Rambam também traça limites. Um gentio não deve guardar um Shabat completo nem inventar uma nova religião ou novos mandamentos. A sucá não entra nessa restrição.

Um detalhe prático: muitos *poskim* (autoridades halachicas) dizem que um gentio não deve recitar a bênção judaica da sucá (*leishev basucá*, "...que nos santificou com Seus mandamentos e nos ordenou..."), porque ele não recebeu essa ordem. Ele pode sentar na sucá, comer nela e pensar no sentido da festa, mas sem essa bênção.

## 3. Ele recebe recompensa?
O Talmud responde que sim, mas com uma diferença:
> שֶׁאֵין מְקַבְּלִין עֲלֵיהֶם שָׂכָר כִּמְצוֶּוה וְעוֹשֶׂה, אֶלָּא כְּמִי שֶׁאֵינוֹ מְצוֶּוה וְעוֹשֶׂה… גָּדוֹל הַמְצוֶּוה וְעוֹשֶׂה יוֹתֵר מִשֶּׁאֵינוֹ מְצוֶּוה וְעוֹשֶׂה
> "Eles não recebem recompensa como quem foi ordenado e cumpre, mas como quem não foi ordenado e cumpre… Maior é quem foi ordenado e cumpre do que quem não foi ordenado e cumpre." [Avodah Zarah 3a]

## 4. A sucá e as nações no futuro (agadá)
Na mesma página, o Talmud conta que, no futuro, as nações pedirão a Deus: "Dá-nos a Torá desde o início, e a cumpriremos!" Deus responde que tem "uma mitsvá fácil, chamada sucá", e diz a elas que a façam. O Talmud explica que ela é chamada fácil porque não custa dinheiro. Cada um constrói sua sucá no telhado. Deus então manda um calor intenso, como o de Tamuz, e cada um sai dando um chute na sua sucá [Avodah Zarah 3a].

Uma leitura possível (interpretação minha): a sucá é um teste de compromisso. A questão não é apenas fazer a mitsvá, mas continuar nela quando fica desconfortável. Nos dias de Sucot, os 70 novilhos oferecidos no Templo correspondiam às 70 nações. Por isso, a festa também tem uma dimensão universal: as nações aparecem nela, embora a obrigação seja só de Israel.

## 5. Observações práticas
- Um judeu pode convidar um amigo gentio para a sua sucá. Mas, em dia de *Yom Tov* (dia festivo), há restrições a cozinhar especialmente para um gentio. Convém perguntar a um rabino como fazer isso.
- Para o gentio interessado na Torá, o caminho principal recomendado é guardar as sete leis de Noé. Mitsvot voluntárias como a sucá vêm além disso.

Para casos concretos, consulte um rabino ortodoxo.

answer:
**Avant de manger une tomate, on dit *Boré peri haadama*, la bénédiction des fruits du sol, et non *Boré peri haets*, celle des fruits d'arbre.** Après avoir mangé, on dit ***Boré néfachot***. C'est la règle chez les Ashkénazes comme chez les Séfarades.

> **Bénédiction avant :** בָּרוּךְ אַתָּה ה' אֱלֹהֵינוּ מֶלֶךְ הָעוֹלָם בּוֹרֵא פְּרִי הָאֲדָמָה
> « Béni sois-Tu, Éternel notre Dieu, Roi du monde, qui crées le fruit du sol. »

## Points clés
- La tomate est un fruit du sol : sa bénédiction est *Boré peri haadama*.
- Une plante n'est un « arbre » que si ses feuilles poussent sur un bois qui reste d'une année à l'autre. Si elles repoussent des racines, c'est un fruit du sol.
- Après en avoir mangé la quantité requise (un *kazayit*, environ 27-30 g), on dit *Boré néfachot*.
- Si la tomate est mangée pendant un repas avec du pain, la bénédiction sur le pain (*hamotsi*) la couvre déjà.

## La source
Le Choulhan Aroukh dit : « על פירות הארץ מברך בורא פרי האדמה ». Traduction : « Sur les fruits de la terre, on dit *Boré peri haadama* » [Shulchan Arukh, Orach Chayim 203:1].

Il donne l'exemple des fraises, qui poussent sur un buisson : leur bénédiction est aussi *haadama* [Shulchan Arukh, Orach Chayim 203:2]. Le Rema, dans son ajout (« הגה »), explique le critère. Une plante ne s'appelle « arbre » que si ses feuilles sortent de son bois. Si elles sortent des racines, ce n'est pas un arbre. C'est le cas des plantes dont la tige disparaît complètement en hiver puis repousse des racines.

La tomate entre clairement dans cette catégorie : c'est une plante annuelle, sans tronc permanent. Toutes les autorités la classent donc parmi les fruits du sol. Dans les climats chauds, un plant de tomate peut parfois vivre plusieurs saisons. Les décisionnaires maintiennent quand même *haadama*, parce que la plante donne des fruits dès sa première année et n'a pas de vrai bois.

## La bénédiction après
Pour les fruits d'arbre (sauf les sept espèces), les fruits du sol et les légumes, la bénédiction finale est *Boré néfachot rabot* [Shulchan Arukh, Orach Chayim 207:1].

## Cas particuliers
- **Salade** : si la tomate est l'ingrédient principal, ou si les légumes sont tous *haadama*, une seule bénédiction *haadama* suffit.
- **Jus de tomate** : en général on dit *Chéhakol*, comme pour le jus de presque tous les fruits.
- **Sauce, purée ou ketchup** : il y a des avis différents. Beaucoup de décisionnaires ashkénazes, dans la ligne du Michna Beroura, disent *Chéhakol* si la tomate est complètement écrasée et méconnaissable. Certains décisionnaires séfarades distinguent selon les cas. En pratique, la sauce est le plus souvent mangée pendant un repas avec du pain, où la question ne se pose pas.

Pour un cas précis, demandez à votre rabbin.

**No: no se puede encender fuego en Shabat.** La Torá lo prohíbe de forma explícita, y encender (*mav'ir*) es una de las 39 *melajot* (labores creativas) prohibidas en Shabat. Hay una sola excepción importante: cuando hay peligro para la vida (*pikuaj néfesh*), no solo está permitido encender fuego, sino que es obligatorio hacerlo.

## Puntos clave
- La Torá dice explícitamente: «No encenderán fuego en ninguna de sus moradas en el día de Shabat».
- La Mishná incluye «el que enciende» entre las 39 labores prohibidas, y el Rambam enseña que se transgrede incluso con un fuego muy pequeño.
- La práctica común entre las autoridades ortodoxas es que encender una luz eléctrica o un aparato también está prohibido en Shabat. Lo que sí se permite es preparar luces o un temporizador antes de que empiece.
- En Iom Tov (días festivos que no caen en Shabat) la regla es distinta. Se puede pasar fuego de una llama ya encendida para cocinar, pero no crear fuego nuevo.
- Si una vida está en peligro, se enciende o se hace lo que sea necesario sin dudar.

## 1. La fuente en la Torá
[Exodus 35:3]: «לֹא־תְבַעֲרוּ אֵשׁ בְּכֹל מֹשְׁבֹתֵיכֶם בְּיוֹם הַשַּׁבָּת» («No encenderán fuego en ninguna de sus moradas en el día de Shabat»; traducción mía).

El Talmud [Shabbat 70a] se pregunta por qué la Torá menciona el fuego por separado, si ya está incluido en la prohibición general de trabajar en Shabat. Hay dos opiniones:
- **Rabí Yosi**: lo menciona para enseñar que encender es una prohibición menos grave (*lelav*), sin la pena capital de otras labores.
- **Rabí Natán**: lo menciona para enseñar que cada labor es una transgresión independiente (*lejalek*).

## 2. Una de las 39 labores
La Mishná [Mishnah Shabbat 7:2] enumera las labores prohibidas y entre ellas incluye «הַמְכַבֶּה וְהַמַּבְעִיר» («el que apaga y el que enciende»).

## 3. La ley según el Rambam
El Rambam [Mishneh Torah, Sabbath 12:1] establece:
- Quien enciende cualquier cantidad de fuego es culpable.
- Lo es tanto si enciende una vela o leña «para calentarse como para iluminar».
- Calentar un metal para templarlo también es una forma derivada de esta labor.

Por eso están prohibidos en Shabat, entre otras cosas: encender velas, fósforos o mecheros, prender la estufa, avivar una llama o fumar.

## 4. ¿Y la electricidad?
Las autoridades ortodoxas aceptadas prohíben encender luces y aparatos eléctricos en Shabat, aunque no coinciden en la razón exacta:
- Una bombilla incandescente se considera fuego en sentido pleno, porque el filamento se pone incandescente.
- El Jazón Ish veía en cerrar un circuito una forma de «construir».
- Otros lo explican como prohibición rabínica de «crear algo nuevo» (*molid*).

Sobre esto hay acuerdo en la práctica entre ashkenazíes, sefaradíes y Jabad. Lo que hacen las comunidades es:
- Encender las velas de Shabat antes de que empiece Shabat.
- Dejar encendidas desde antes las luces que se necesiten.
- Usar temporizadores programados antes de Shabat.
- Mantener la comida caliente con una placa o *blej* encendidos de antemano. Esto tiene reglas propias.

## 5. Iom Tov: una diferencia importante
En los días festivos se permite cocinar y, por eso, usar el fuego. Sin embargo, el Shulján Aruj [Shulchan Arukh, Orach Chayim 502:1] dice: «אין מוציאין האש... לא מן העצים ולא מן האבנים» («No se produce fuego nuevo, ni de maderas ni de piedras»). Por eso:
- Se puede pasar el fuego de una llama que ya está encendida, por ejemplo desde una vela que arde desde antes de Iom Tov.
- No se puede crear fuego nuevo con un fósforo o un encendedor.

Esto vale solo para Iom Tov. **En Shabat, incluso pasar fuego de una llama a otra está prohibido.**

## 6. Peligro para la vida
El Shulján Aruj [Shulchan Arukh, Orach Chayim 328:2] es tajante: «מי שיש לו חולי של סכנה מצוה לחלל עליו את השבת, והזריז הרי זה משובח, והשואל הרי זה שופך דמים» («Por quien tiene una enfermedad peligrosa es un precepto profanar el Shabat; quien se apresura es digno de alabanza, y quien se detiene a preguntar es como un derramador de sangre»).

Si alguien necesita luz, calor o cualquier otra cosa por un riesgo real para su vida, por ejemplo un bebé o un anciano expuestos a un frío peligroso, se actúa de inmediato.

Para situaciones de incomodidad sin peligro, a veces se permite pedir ayuda a una persona no judía. Esto tiene reglas detalladas: no es una autorización general y conviene preguntarlo con antelación.

Si me dices tu caso concreto (en Shabat o en Iom Tov, una vela, la estufa, la luz eléctrica), puedo explicarte en detalle cómo lo tratan las fuentes. **Para tu situación personal, consulta con tu rabino.**

**Réponse courte :** pour un couple marié, la loi talmudique de base est permissive : « tout ce qu'un homme veut faire avec sa femme, il peut le faire ». Mais le Choulhan Aroukh de Rabbi Yossef Karo (le *Mehaber*), que suivent les Séfarades, **interdit explicitement** d'embrasser les parties intimes de la femme. La pratique séfarade standard est donc de s'en abstenir. Le Rema, que suivent les Ashkénazes, le permet légalement, tout en recommandant la retenue.

## Points clés
- Le Talmud rejette l'avis strict de Yohanan ben Dahabaï et autorise au couple toute forme d'intimité [Nedarim 20a-b].
- Le Rambam le permet aussi explicitement, mais il ajoute qu'il est pieux de se sanctifier [Mishneh Torah, Forbidden Intercourse 21:9].
- Le Mehaber l'interdit et y voit une transgression de plusieurs versets [Shulchan Arukh, Orach Chayim 240:4]. C'est la référence des Séfarades.
- Le Rema (pour les Ashkénazes) le permet, en présentant l'abstention comme une sainteté supplémentaire [Shulchan Arukh, Even HaEzer 25:2].
- Tout cela ne concerne que des époux, et seulement pendant les périodes où la femme est permise à son mari (pas pendant la période de *nidda*, l'impureté menstruelle).

## 1. La source talmudique
Rabbi Yohanan ben Dahabaï rapporte que des anges lui ont révélé certaines causes de handicaps chez les enfants. Selon lui, les enfants naissent muets « parce que [les parents] embrassent cet endroit » (« מִפְּנֵי שֶׁמְּנַשְּׁקִים עַל אוֹתוֹ מָקוֹם »). Mais la Guemara conclut :

> « אֵין הֲלָכָה כְּיוֹחָנָן בֶּן דַּהֲבַאי, אֶלָּא כֹּל מַה שֶּׁאָדָם רוֹצֶה לַעֲשׂוֹת בְּאִשְׁתּוֹ — עוֹשֶׂה »
> « La halakha n'est pas selon Yohanan ben Dahabaï ; tout ce qu'un homme veut faire avec sa femme, il le fait » [Nedarim 20a-b] (ma traduction).

La Guemara illustre cela par la viande achetée chez le boucher : on peut la manger salée, rôtie ou cuite, comme on le souhaite.

## 2. Le Rambam
Le Rambam écrit que l'homme peut « embrasser tout membre qu'il désire » (« וּמְנַשֵּׁק בְּכָל אֵיבָר וְאֵיבָר שֶׁיִּרְצֶה »), à condition de ne pas émettre de semence en vain. Il ajoute qu'il relève de la *midat hassidout* (la piété) de ne pas se conduire avec légèreté et de se sanctifier pendant les relations [Mishneh Torah, Forbidden Intercourse 21:9].

## 3. La position séfarade : le Mehaber
Dans les lois sur la conduite intime, le Mehaber tranche :

> « אסור להסתכל באותו מקום... וכל שכן הנושק שם שעובר על כל אלה ועוד שעובר על בל תשקצו את נפשותיכם »
> « Il est interdit de regarder cet endroit… à plus forte raison celui qui l'embrasse transgresse tout cela, et transgresse en outre "ne rendez pas vos âmes abominables" » [Shulchan Arukh, Orach Chayim 240:4].

- **La source :** le Be'er HaGolah indique que cette règle vient du Raavad, dans le *Chaar HaKedoucha* de son livre *Baalé HaNéfech*.
- **Pourquoi interdire malgré la conclusion du Talmud ?** Le Gaon de Vilna l'explique [Beur HaGra on Shulchan Arukh, Orach Chayim 240:4:1]. Selon lui, les Sages ne contestaient Yohanan ben Dahabaï que sur la manière d'avoir des relations (« renverser la table »). Ils n'auraient pas contesté ses autres points, dont le baiser à cet endroit.
- **Le Kaf HaHaïm**, un décisionnaire séfarade majeur, commente ce passage dans la lignée du Mehaber [Kaf HaChayim on Shulchan Arukh, Orach Chayim 240:40:1]. Les sources kabbalistiques, très influentes chez les Séfarades, renforcent cette rigueur.
- **En pratique :** à ma connaissance, les décisionnaires séfarades suivent en général le Mehaber sur ce point. C'est donc considéré comme interdit, et non comme une simple question de piété. Je n'ai pas pu vérifier directement les écrits de Rav Ovadia Yossef ou du Yalkout Yossef sur ce sujet précis. Certains rabbins séfarades contemporains peuvent avoir des nuances, à vérifier auprès d'eux.

## 4. Pour comparaison : la pratique ashkénaze
Dans une glose qui commence par « הגה », le Rema écrit que l'homme « peut faire avec sa femme ce qu'il veut… et embrasser tout membre qu'il désire » (« ומנשק בכל אבר שירצה »). Il ajoute aussitôt : « כל המקדש עצמו במותר לו קדוש יאמרו לו », c'est-à-dire « celui qui se sanctifie dans ce qui lui est permis sera appelé saint » [Shulchan Arukh, Even HaEzer 25:2]. Selon cet avis, c'est donc permis, mais l'abstention est louable. Certains, comme le Gaon de Vilna cité plus haut, penchent toutefois vers la rigueur même pour les Ashkénazes.

## 5. Les cadres qui s'appliquent dans tous les cas
- **Uniquement entre époux.** Hors mariage, la question ne se pose pas : les relations intimes sont interdites.
- **Pas pendant la *nidda*.** Tout contact intime est alors interdit, jusqu'au bain rituel (*mikvé*).
- **Le consentement et la tendresse.** Il faut le consentement plein des deux, et le mari ne doit avoir de relations qu'avec l'accord de sa femme [Shulchan Arukh, Even HaEzer 25:2].
- **La pudeur.** Les relations doivent rester dans la pudeur (*tsniout*) et l'intimité du couple.

Si votre couple suit la tradition séfarade et que cette question vous concerne concrètement, parlez-en discrètement à votre rav. Il connaît votre tradition familiale et peut répondre avec les nuances voulues. C'est un sujet légitime qu'un rabbin a l'habitude de traiter avec délicatesse.

**Non, la Torah n'interdit pas le mariage entre cousins.** La liste des unions interdites (*arayot*) en [Leviticus 18] ne mentionne pas les cousins. La Torah raconte même plusieurs mariages entre cousins, chez les Patriarches et ailleurs. La tradition rabbinique va plus loin : elle considère comme une bonne chose d'épouser sa nièce, un lien encore plus proche.

## Points essentiels
- Les cousins ne figurent pas parmi les unions interdites de [Leviticus 18] et [Leviticus 20].
- Jacob a épousé Rachel et Léa, ses cousines germaines. Les filles de Tselofhad ont épousé leurs cousins, sur l'ordre de Dieu transmis par Moïse.
- Le Talmud, le Rambam et le Rema vont jusqu'à recommander le mariage avec sa nièce.
- Certaines autorités recommandent d'éviter les unions avec la nièce. Aujourd'hui, on conseille souvent un dépistage génétique : c'est une précaution, pas une interdiction.

## 1. Ce que dit la Torah
La Torah énumère les proches parents interdits : mère, sœur, tante, belle-fille, belle-sœur, etc. Les cousins n'en font pas partie, et ce qui n'est pas interdit est permis.

Les récits bibliques le confirment :
- **Jacob et Rachel.** Le verset souligne que Rachel est la fille de Laban, le frère de sa mère : « וַיְהִי כַּאֲשֶׁר רָאָה יַעֲקֹב אֶת־רָחֵל בַּת־לָבָן אֲחִי אִמּוֹ » (« Lorsque Jacob vit Rachel, fille de Laban, frère de sa mère… ») [Genesis 29:10]. Léa et Rachel étaient donc ses cousines germaines.
- **Isaac et Rébecca.** Rébecca était la petite-fille de Nahor, le frère d'Abraham. C'est donc une proche cousine d'Isaac.
- **Les filles de Tselofhad.** Pour que leur héritage reste dans la tribu, elles se marient selon l'ordre divin : « לִבְנֵי דֹדֵיהֶן לְנָשִׁים » (« elles devinrent les épouses des fils de leurs oncles ») [Numbers 36:11]. Ici, le mariage entre cousins répond directement à un commandement transmis par Moïse.

## 2. La tradition rabbinique : encore plus permissive
- **Le Talmud** [Yevamot 62b] fait l'éloge de celui qui épouse la fille de sa sœur. Il s'appuie sur le verset « וּמִבְּשָׂרְךָ לֹא תִתְעַלָּם » (« ne te dérobe pas à ta propre chair ») d'Isaïe 58:7.
- **Le Rambam** écrit : « וּמִצְוַת חֲכָמִים שֶׁיִּשָּׂא אָדָם בַּת אֲחוֹתוֹ וְהוּא הַדִּין לְבַת אָחִיו ». Traduction : « C'est une prescription des Sages qu'un homme épouse la fille de sa sœur, et il en va de même pour la fille de son frère » [Mishneh Torah, Forbidden Intercourse 2:14].
- **Dans le Choulhan Aroukh**, cette recommandation ne se trouve pas dans le texte principal de Rabbi Yossef Karo. Elle vient de la glose du **Rema** (qui fait autorité chez les ashkénazes) : c'est une *mitsva* d'épouser la fille de sa sœur, et certains disent aussi celle de son frère [Shulchan Arukh, Even HaEzer 2:6].

Si le mariage avec une nièce est autorisé et même encouragé, le mariage entre cousins, un lien plus éloigné, l'est à plus forte raison.

## 3. Nuances et précautions
- **Le Testament de Rabbi Yehouda HaHassid** (Allemagne, XIIᵉ–XIIIᵉ siècle) déconseille d'épouser sa nièce. Plusieurs décisionnaires ashkénazes ont tenu compte de cette mise en garde. Elle ne concerne pas les cousins, et il s'agit d'une prudence, pas d'une interdiction de la Torah.
- **La santé.** Le risque de maladies génétiques récessives est plus élevé chez des cousins germains. Le principe de préservation de la vie et de la santé (*chmirat haguf*, *pikoua'h néfech*) a une grande importance en halakha. C'est pourquoi beaucoup de rabbins encouragent aujourd'hui les couples apparentés à faire un dépistage génétique, par exemple via Dor Yeshorim dans les communautés orthodoxes. C'est un conseil de prudence, non une loi.
- **La loi civile.** Certains pays ou États interdisent le mariage entre cousins. Dans ces endroits, le principe *dina dé-malkhouta dina* (« la loi du royaume est la loi ») peut entrer en jeu.

## 4. En pratique
- **Ashkénazes et séfarades** sont d'accord : le mariage entre cousins germains est entièrement permis par la halakha.
- **Pour la nièce**, la recommandation du Rema s'applique aux ashkénazes. En pratique, on tient souvent compte de la mise en garde de Rabbi Yehouda HaHassid, et le Rema n'en fait pas un usage établi.

Pour un cas personnel, et notamment pour les aspects médicaux, consultez votre rabbin (et un conseiller en génétique).

answer:
I couldn't find any source that discusses sinks under that name. They're a modern fixture, so Torah talks about them in two indirect ways:

- **Practical halacha (Jewish law):** a sink with a drain takes care of older rules about where you may pour water. It also brings new questions, mostly about Shabbat and kashrut (kosher law).
- **Inspiration:** the model for every sink is the *kiyor*, the copper washbasin in the Mishkan (Tabernacle) where the priests washed their hands and feet. It carries some of the most moving teachings in the Torah.

## Key Takeaways
- Several rules depended on where used water lands: not on the ground, not where people walk, not on plants on Shabbat, not into a small courtyard that drains into the street. A sink drain solves most of these quietly.
- An old ruling about water let out of a hole in a barrel is the starting point for whether you can wash for bread straight from a tap.
- Sinks also raise new Shabbat and kashrut questions: hot taps, sponges, drain strainers, and meat versus dairy.
- The *kiyor* was made from the women's copper mirrors. Rashi teaches that God treasured them above all the other gifts.
- In the Second Temple, Ben Katin improved the *kiyor* with twelve spouts and a mechanism to keep its water fresh overnight. He was the first "plumber" the Mishnah praises.

---

## Part 1: Problems a sink solves

### 1. Where to pour the morning hand-washing water
The Shulchan Arukh (Mechaber) rules:
> "מים של נט"י שחרית אסור ליהנות מהם ולא ישפכם בבית ולא במקום שעוברים שם בני אדם"
> "You may not benefit from the water used for the morning hand-washing. Don't pour it out in the house or anywhere people pass." [Shulchan Arukh, Orach Chayim 4:9]

The concern is the *ru'ach ra'ah* (impure spirit) that rests on the hands at night and passes into the water. Before indoor plumbing, people had to collect this water and carry it outside to a place no one walked. A drain sends it straight into a closed pipe that no one touches or steps over. Ashkenazim and Sephardim both follow this ruling. Many people still wash into a basin or into the sink itself so the water goes right down the drain.

### 2. *Mayim acharonim* (washing after a meal)
> "מים אחרונים אין נוטלין על גבי קרקע אלא בכלי מפני רוח רעה ששורה עליהם"
> "*Mayim acharonim* is not done over the ground but into a vessel, because a harmful spirit rests on the water." [Shulchan Arukh, Orach Chayim 181:2]

If you have no vessel, you may wash over thin pieces of wood. Many people wash *mayim acharonim* over a sink, since the drain takes the water away. Some still prefer a small dish at the table, which is the more literal "vessel."

### 3. Shabbat: not watering plants by accident
Washing your hands outdoors on Shabbat over grass or plants is forbidden. It waters them (*zore'a*, sowing), and since that result can't be avoided, it counts even though you didn't intend it (*pesik reisha*) [Shulchan Arukh, Orach Chayim 336:3]. The Rema adds that it's best not to eat in a garden at all if water will be used, because it's hard to keep drops from falling. Washing at a sink takes away this whole worry.

### 4. Shabbat: water that flows into the public domain
The Mishnah and Gemara (Eruvin chapter 8, around 88a) deal with dirty water poured into a small courtyard. The Shulchan Arukh rules that if a courtyard is smaller than 4×4 *amot* (cubits) and borders a public domain, you may not pour water into it on summer Shabbatot. The ground can't absorb the roughly two *se'ah* of water a household uses each day, so it is "as if he pours into the public domain." The fix is to dig a pit that holds two *se'ah*. The Rema adds that if the pit is outside the courtyard, it must be covered with boards [Shulchan Arukh, Orach Chayim 357:1].

A household sink is a hidden version of that pit and drain. The water goes into a closed pipe, not into an open street. This is my explanation; I couldn't retrieve a modern ruling that says it in these words. Contemporary poskim (halachic authorities) generally treat pouring into an ordinary sink on Shabbat as plainly permitted. How the water travels through pipes doesn't create the old concern.

### 5. Washing for bread straight from a tap
This is an issue the sink itself raises. Washing for bread requires the water to come by *ko'ach gavra* (human force). The Mechaber rules that if water runs out of a barrel's hole by itself, washing under it is invalid. But if you pull out a stopper and catch the water, that counts as *ko'ach gavra*. You have to replace and remove the stopper for each pour [Shulchan Arukh, Orach Chayim 159:9].

Later authorities discuss whether opening a faucet works like pulling the stopper. The common and preferred practice for both Ashkenazim and Sephardim is to wash with a cup, and many people keep a two-handled washing cup by the sink for that reason. Ask your rabbi before relying on a tap alone.

## Part 2: New questions a sink brings

- **Washing dishes on Shabbat.** You may wash dishes only if they are needed for later that Shabbat. After *seudah shelishit* (the third meal) you may not, though drinking cups may be washed all day [Shulchan Arukh, Orach Chayim 323:6]. Separately, many people avoid ordinary sponges because of *sechitah* (squeezing out liquid) and use a brush or a special Shabbat sponge.
- **The hot tap.** With many water heaters, opening the hot tap brings cold water into the tank, where it gets cooked. Many authorities therefore forbid using the hot tap on Shabbat. Some heating systems may be different, so ask about your own setup. On Yom Tov (festival days), warming water for hands and face is generally allowed, unlike bathing the whole body.
- **The drain strainer.** Peninei Halakhah rules that you may empty food scraps from a sink strainer on Shabbat, with no need to do it in an unusual way. Clearing dirt doesn't "fix" anything; it just removes filth [Peninei Halakhah, Shabbat 15:9:8; Peninei Halakhah, Shabbat 23:12:5].
- **Kashrut.** Hot water and food bits in a shared sink can pass taste between meat and dairy. Common solutions are separate sinks, or a single sink with separate basins or racks for meat and dairy and no dishes resting on the sink itself. Customs and needs vary, and a mix-up that has already happened is a question for a rabbi. Sinks also need to be cleaned and often kashered (made kosher) for Pesach.

## Part 3: Inspiring Torah: the *kiyor*, the first sink

### Mirrors turned into a basin
The Torah says the *kiyor* was made "from the mirrors of the women who gathered" (Exodus 38:8). Rashi, based on Midrash Tanchuma, says Moshe wanted to turn the mirrors down because they were tools of vanity. God told him:
> "קַבֵּל, כִּי אֵלּוּ חֲבִיבִין עָלַי מִן הַכֹּל"
> "Accept them, for these are dearer to Me than everything else."

In Egypt, the women brought food to their exhausted husbands. They used these mirrors to wake their love, and so they kept the Jewish people alive and raised "huge hosts" of children. That's why the *kiyor* was made from them: its water was used to bring peace between husband and wife in the *sotah* ritual (when a husband suspected his wife) [Rashi on Exodus 38:8].

**A thought for today (my own reflection):** many of our sinks have a mirror right above them. The Torah's first sink was made from mirrors. When you wash in the morning and catch your reflection, you can ask the question the *kiyor* asks: is my self-image serving me alone, or is it building love, family, and *kedushah* (holiness)? Even a "vain" object becomes holy when it's used for love and for building others.

### Wash before you serve
The priests had to wash their hands and feet from the *kiyor* before serving in the Mishkan (Exodus 30:17–21). This is the root of our morning *netilat yadayim* (hand-washing), which tradition explains as preparing each day as a fresh service of God. Every trip to the sink before davening (praying) or eating bread is a small echo of the priests at the *kiyor*.

### Ben Katin, the engineer the Mishnah praises
> "בֶּן קָטִין עָשָׂה שְׁנֵים עָשָׂר דַּד לַכִּיּוֹר, שֶׁלֹּא הָיוּ לוֹ אֶלָּא שְׁנַיִם. וְאַף הוּא עָשָׂה מוּכְנִי לַכִּיּוֹר, שֶׁלֹּא יִהְיוּ מֵימָיו נִפְסָלִין בְּלִינָה"
> "Ben Katin made twelve spigots for the *kiyor*, which had only two, and he made a *mukheni* (mechanism) so its water would not become disqualified by staying overnight." [Mishnah Yoma 3:10] (See the Gemara's discussion in Yoma 37a.)

Two lessons come from this:
- **Making room for others.** With twelve spigots, many priests could wash at once, so no one had to wait and service didn't slow down. Good design is a form of *chesed* (kindness).
- **Staying fresh.** The mechanism lowered the basin into flowing water at night so its water was never "stale." Our spiritual life needs the same: water that stays connected to its living source is renewed every morning (compare Lamentations 3:23, "new every morning").

The Mishnah mentions Ben Katin among those "remembered for praise." Practical skill, plumbing included, becomes holy when it serves God and others.

### The drain and *teshuvah* (returning to God)
The prophet promises: "I will sprinkle pure water upon you and you shall be purified" (Ezekiel 36:25). Rabbi Akiva teaches that God is the *mikveh* (ritual bath) of Israel [Yoma 85b]. A sink pictures this simply: water washes off the day's dirt, and the drain carries it away for good. Through sincere *teshuvah*, what we wash off doesn't have to stay with us.

Practical details differ between communities and between kitchens, so please consult your rabbi for your own situation.

answer:
I couldn't find any source in Chazal about the sink as we know it: a basin with a tap and a drain plumbed into the house. They did, though, discuss most of its parts and the problems they cause: waste water on Shabbat (the *ukah*, a pit for waste water, and the *biv*, a drain), hand-washing water (the Temple laver, *mayim acharonim*, and watering plants on Shabbat), and drainage (the Temple's own drain system). Read together, these sources show which old problems an indoor sink tied into a sewer quietly solves.

## Key Takeaways
- Pouring waste water on Shabbat was a real problem. If the water ran from a small courtyard into the public domain, it could count as carrying (*hotza'ah*), so Chazal required a pit holding two *se'ah* [Mishnah Eruvin 8:9].
- Rabba gives the reason: a household uses about two *se'ah* of water a day. That makes the *ukah* an early "drain sized to daily use" [Eruvin 88a].
- Washing hands outdoors over grass on Shabbat is forbidden as watering plants, because the result is unavoidable (*psik reisha*) [Shulchan Arukh, Orach Chayim 336:3]. An indoor sink avoids the problem.
- The Temple had something close to a plumbed washstand: Ben Katin's twelve spigots and the *mukheni* machine for the laver [Mishnah Yoma 3:10], plus a drain carrying blood out to the Kidron [Mishnah Middot 3:2].
- A modern sink also raises new Shabbat questions, such as squeezing a sponge, hot water from the tap, and drain strainers. Those are treated by later authorities, not Chazal.

---

## 1. Waste water on Shabbat: the *ukah* and the *biv*

**The Mishnah** [Mishnah Eruvin 8:9]:
> חָצֵר שֶׁהִיא פְחוּתָה מֵאַרְבַּע אַמּוֹת, אֵין שׁוֹפְכִין בְּתוֹכָהּ מַיִם בְּשַׁבָּת, אֶלָּא אִם כֵּן עָשׂוּ לָהּ עוּקָה מַחֲזֶקֶת סָאתַיִם מִן הַנֶּקֶב וּלְמַטָּה
> "A courtyard smaller than four cubits: one may not pour water into it on Shabbat unless a pit was made for it that holds two *se'ah* from the opening down."

If the pit is dug outside, in the public domain, it must be covered over. That way the water lands in an exempt area (*makom petur*), not straight into the public domain.

**The drain (*biv*):** Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov allows pouring water into a drain that runs covered for four cubits under the public domain. The Sages disagree: even from a roof or courtyard a hundred cubits big, you may not pour straight into the mouth of the drain. You may pour it onto the roof and let it run down into the drain by itself [Mishnah Eruvin 8:10].

**The Gemara's reasoning** [Eruvin 88a–88b]:
- **Rabba:** "אָדָם עָשׂוּי לְהִסְתַּפֵּק סָאתַיִם מַיִם בְּכׇל יוֹם" ("a person typically uses two *se'ah* of water every day"). In a courtyard of four by four cubits, people want to sprinkle the water to settle the dust. In a smaller one they just dump it, so it flows out.
- **Rabbi Zeira:** the question is absorption. Four square cubits of ground soak the water up (*tayimi*). Less than that does not.
- **Chananya** (a dissenting view): even on a big roof one may not pour, "לְפִי שֶׁאֵין הַגָּג עָשׂוּי לִבְלוֹעַ, אֶלָּא לְקַלֵּחַ" ("a roof is made to drain, not to absorb"). In other words, a surface built to drain sends the water onward by design.
- **Rainy season:** pouring is allowed. Abaye's reason is that the courtyard is already muddy. Also, no one will say "So-and-so's gutter is running on Shabbat," because "סְתָם צִנּוֹרוֹת מְקַלְּחִים הֵם" ("gutters normally run" in winter). Abaye concludes that in that season one may pour even a *kor* or two [Eruvin 88b].

**Codified:** [Shulchan Arukh, Orach Chayim 357:1] rules this way for a courtyard next to the public domain. The Rema adds the size of the pit: half a cubit by half a cubit, three-fifths of a cubit deep. He also notes that next to a *karmelit* (a semi-public area) no pit is needed at all.

**What the sink solves:** An indoor sink connected to a sewer means waste water never pours out into the open. It goes into a closed pipe, much like the covered *biv* or the *ukah*. Later authorities still discuss pipes that empty into a public area, but for most homes the sink has made this whole sugya a background issue.

## 2. Hand-washing water and plants on Shabbat

[Shulchan Arukh, Orach Chayim 336:3]: people eating in a garden may not wash their hands over grass. Even though they don't intend to water it, the result is unavoidable (*psik reisha*). The Rema advises not eating in a garden at all if water will be used there, because it is hard to keep it from spilling. A sink indoors removes the problem completely.

## 3. *Mayim acharonim*: into a vessel, not onto the ground

A baraita discussed in [Chullin 105a–105b] says first waters may be poured onto the ground or into a vessel, but final waters (*mayim acharonim*) only into a vessel. The reason given for the obligation of final waters is "Sodomite salt," which can blind if it gets in the eyes [Chullin 105b]. The classic commentators explain that the water poured off afterward carries something harmful, so it should be caught rather than left on the floor. Later authorities discuss whether a sink basin counts as a "vessel" for this.

## 4. The Temple's "sink": the laver (*kiyor*)

[Mishnah Yoma 3:10] (also [Yoma 37a]):
> בֶּן קָטִין עָשָׂה שְׁנֵים עָשָׂר דַּד לַכִּיּוֹר, שֶׁלֹּא הָיוּ לוֹ אֶלָּא שְׁנַיִם. וְאַף הוּא עָשָׂה מוּכְנִי לַכִּיּוֹר, שֶׁלֹּא יִהְיוּ מֵימָיו נִפְסָלִין בְּלִינָה
> "Ben Katin made twelve spigots for the laver, which had had only two. He also made a *mukheni* (machine) for the laver, so that its water would not become disqualified by staying overnight."

Some points worth noticing:
- **Spigots:** with twelve taps, many kohanim could wash hands and feet at once. It was a fix for congestion.
- **The *mukheni*:** water that sat in the laver overnight became unfit (*linah*). The machine lowered the laver into a cistern of water at night, so its water stayed part of the larger body of water. The idea of water that never sits still, like running tap water, is a real halachic principle here.
- **Credit for improvements:** the Mishnah says the people "would mention them favorably." Chazal praise someone who invents a better tool for avodah. The Mishnah in Tamid also says the sound of the *mukheni* could be heard as far away as Jericho.

## 5. The Temple's drainage

[Mishnah Middot 3:2]: at the southwest corner of the altar there were two small holes "like two thin nostrils." The blood poured on the base ran down through them, mixed in the channel (*ammah*), and flowed out to the Kidron valley. So the Mikdash itself had a built drainage system.

## 6. Washing dishes on Shabbat and Yom Tov

A baraita in Shabbat 118a allows washing plates on Shabbat only when they are needed for a later meal that day. After the last meal you may not wash them, because that would be preparing for after Shabbat. Cups may be washed all day, since people drink at any time. I'm paraphrasing that passage from memory; I wasn't able to pull up its exact text. A sink doesn't change this rule, but it makes it easy to keep: rinse only what you need.

## 7. New questions the sink created

These come from later authorities, not Chazal. They show that every convenience brings its own questions:
- **Squeezing (*sechitah*)** a sponge or dishcloth.
- **Hot water from the tap**, which may draw cold water into a heater (*bishul*, cooking).
- **A drain strainer**, which may involve *borer* (separating).
- **Bar soap**, which may involve *memare'ach* (smoothing).
- **Kashrut:** meat and dairy sharing one sink, or washing with hot water. This is a whole topic of its own in modern responsa.

## A thought to take away

Rabba's estimate of two *se'ah* a day may be one of the earliest recorded measures of household water use. Chazal sized the pit to that daily amount, so the law matches how people actually live. The Gemara's point about the rainy season adds something too: because gutters normally run in winter, nobody will suspect wrongdoing. In this sugya, halacha pays attention both to what really happens to the water and to how it looks to the neighbors.

For practical questions about using a sink on Shabbat (sponges, hot water, strainers), please ask your rabbi about your own case.

answer:
The app itself isn't forbidden, but for most processed foods you can't rely on an ingredient scan to decide that a product is kosher. Mainstream poskim and kashrut agencies agree that a printed ingredient list doesn't show many things that decide kashrut. A scan can tell you a product is *not* kosher (for example, it lists lard or carmine). It can't tell you a product *is* kosher. For that you generally need a reliable *hechsher* (kosher certification), apart from a short list of simple items that recognized agencies say need none.

## Key Takeaways
- An ingredient list doesn't show the factory equipment, processing aids, or where "natural flavors" and similar items came from, and all of these can make a food non-kosher.
- In some cases even a tiny amount of a forbidden ingredient makes the whole product forbidden. A rennet or setting agent (*davar ha-ma'amid*) is the classic example, so you can't assume tiny amounts cancel out.
- Some laws have nothing to do with ingredients: food cooked by a non-Jew (*bishul akum*), bread baked by a non-Jew (*pat akum*), dairy (*chalav Yisrael*), and Jewish-owned chametz kept over Pesach. A scanner can't check any of these.
- An app is a different matter if it looks products up in a database run by a reliable kashrut agency. Then you're relying on that agency, not on the label.

## Why an ingredient list isn't enough

**1. Factory equipment.** A factory's pots and lines absorb flavor from what is cooked in them, and they can pass it into the next product. The Shulchan Arukh rules that a non-Jew's utensils are presumed not to have been used in the last 24 hours. Because of that, food cooked in them is permitted only after the fact (*b'dieved*) [Shulchan Arukh, Yoreh De'ah 122:6]. You aren't allowed to plan on using them. Factories run hot production lines continuously, often on the same day for meat, dairy, and non-kosher products. A label never mentions this.

**2. Ingredients that don't cancel out.** The Rema rules that a forbidden ingredient used as a setting agent isn't nullified even in a thousand times its amount: "דבר האסור בעצמו ומעמיד אפילו באלף לא בטיל" [Shulchan Arukh, Yoreh De'ah 87:11]. Modern equivalents include animal rennet, enzymes, gelatin, and some emulsifiers. Labels often call these by vague names, or leave them out entirely when they count legally as "processing aids."

**3. Deliberate small amounts.** You might think a trace ingredient is cancelled because the product has 60 times more permitted food (*bitul b'shishim*). But the Shulchan Arukh rules: "אין מבטלין איסור לכתחלה" ("one may not deliberately nullify a forbidden substance") [Shulchan Arukh, Yoreh De'ah 99:5]. A manufacturer adds flavorings and additives on purpose, so later authorities debate at length whether nullification even applies. An app that ignores small ingredients is taking one side of a hard question.

**4. Hidden origins.** Glycerin, mono- and diglycerides, "natural flavors," stearic acid, and similar items can come from plants or animals. Some flavorings come from grape products, which raise the separate issue of non-Jewish wine (*stam yeinam*). The label usually doesn't say which source was used.

## Laws an ingredient list can't check
- **Bishul akum (food cooked by a non-Jew):** the communities differ on what Jewish involvement is needed. In the Shulchan Arukh's laws of bishul akum, the Mechaber's standard is generally followed by Sephardim and is stricter than the Rema's, which Ashkenazim follow.
- **Pat akum (bread baked by a non-Jew):** bread from a non-Jewish commercial bakery (*pat palter*) is permitted in some cases. Many people are strict about it, especially during the Ten Days of Repentance (*Aseret Yemei Teshuvah*).
- **Chalav Yisrael (milk supervised by a Jew):** Rav Moshe Feinstein (Igrot Moshe) allowed relying on government regulation of milk. Many people, including Chabad as standard practice, follow the stricter view and require supervision.
- **Chametz she'avar alav ha-Pesach:** chametz owned by a Jew during Pesach remains forbidden afterward, and this depends on who owned the product, not on what is in it.

## Is a label trustworthy at all?
In halacha, a non-Jew's statement is generally accepted about a kashrut matter only when he says it in passing, without knowing anyone relies on it (*mesiach lefi tumo*). Even that was limited. The Shulchan Arukh lets a non-Jew taste a mixture, but the Rema notes: "ואין נוהגים עכשיו לסמוך אעובד כוכבים" ("nowadays we do not customarily rely on the non-Jew") [Shulchan Arukh, Yoreh De'ah 98:1]. Some contemporary poskim give government-mandated labels some weight, since false labeling carries legal penalties. Even so, they generally use labels to *rule a product out*, not to approve it. A label lists what is legally required, not what kashrut requires.

## What's acceptable in practice
- **Products that don't need certification.** The major agencies (OU, Star-K, cRc, and others) publish lists of items that are fine without a hechsher. Examples include raw fruits and vegetables, plain unflavored items, and certain basic products, which vary by country. This judgment comes from the agency's knowledge of how the product is made, not from reading the label.
- **Apps run by agencies.** Several kashrut organizations have apps that check barcodes or certification symbols against their own databases. Using one of these is just a convenient way of relying on that agency's supervision, which is legitimate.
- **Ingredient-reading apps.** These are fine for spotting products that are clearly not kosher, or for allergy-style screening. They aren't a basis for eating a processed product. This holds the same way for Ashkenazim, Sephardim, and Chabad. Chabad adds its own stringencies, such as chalav Yisrael and pat Yisrael, that a scan can never check.

If you tell me which app you have in mind, or which country you live in (rules for products without a hechsher differ from place to place), I can be more specific. For your own case, please consult your rabbi.

answer:
**Short answer:** Between a husband and wife, classical halacha allows anal intercourse in principle. The Talmud, the Rambam and the Rema's gloss on the Shulchan Arukh all say this. There are firm conditions: both spouses must truly consent, and the man must not ejaculate outside the vagina, though a minority view is more lenient on that point. Many authorities, especially in the Kabbalistic and Sephardi traditions, strongly discourage it even though it is technically allowed. Outside marriage, and between two men, it is forbidden.

## Key Takeaways
- **Within marriage it is permitted in principle.** The Rambam and the Rema both rule that a man may have intercourse with his wife "בין כדרכה בין שלא כדרכה" ("whether in the usual way or not").
- **No ejaculation outside the vagina.** The main view forbids it. Some lenient opinions allow it if it happens only occasionally.
- **Her full consent is required.** Nothing is permitted without the wife's willing agreement.
- **Holiness and restraint.** The codes themselves praise holding back even from what is allowed. Some later authorities and the Kabbalistic tradition are much stricter.
- **Outside marriage it is forbidden.** Between men it falls under the explicit Torah prohibition in Leviticus 18:22.

## The Talmudic basis
In Tractate Nedarim, Rabbi Yochanan, speaking for the Sages, rules that "whatever a man wishes to do with his wife, he may do." He compares it to meat from the butcher, which may be prepared however one likes. The Gemara then tells of a woman who complained to Rebbi that her husband had "overturned the table," a euphemism for non-standard intercourse. Rebbi answered that the Torah permits it. (This is in Nedarim 20b. I couldn't retrieve the text just now, so I'm paraphrasing.) A minority opinion there, from Rabbi Yochanan ben Dahavai, warned against such practices. The halacha does not follow it.

## The codes
**Rambam** [Mishneh Torah, Forbidden Intercourse 21:9]:
> "כָּל מַה שֶּׁאָדָם רוֹצֶה לַעֲשׂוֹת בְּאִשְׁתּוֹ עוֹשֶׂה... וּבָא עָלֶיהָ כְּדַרְכָּהּ וְשֶׁלֹּא כְּדַרְכָּהּ, וּבִלְבַד שֶׁלֹּא יוֹצִיא שִׁכְבַת זֶרַע לְבַטָּלָה"
> "A man may do whatever he desires with his wife… vaginal or anal intercourse, provided he does not release seed in vain."

He then adds that it is *middat chassidut* (pious conduct) not to treat these matters lightly. A person should sanctify himself during relations and not stray from "the ordinary way of the world."

**Shulchan Arukh** [Shulchan Arukh, Even HaEzer 25:2]:
- **Mechaber (Rabbi Yosef Karo):** In this se'if he discusses only modest speech and conduct between husband and wife. He does not address this question here.
- **Rema (Rabbi Moshe Isserles), in his gloss (*hagah*):** He follows the Tur. A man may come to his wife "בין כדרכה בין שלא כדרכה," as long as he does not waste seed.
  - He then cites "some who are lenient" (the Tur, quoting the Ri). They allow ejaculation during anal intercourse if it happens occasionally and is not his habit.
  - He ends: "כל המקדש עצמו במותר לו קדוש יאמרו לו" ("whoever sanctifies himself in what is permitted to him is called holy").
  - In the same gloss he rules that a man may not have relations without his wife's consent. If she isn't willing, he must win her over until she is.

## Differences between communities
- **Ashkenazi:** The Rema's gloss is the basis. It is technically permitted under the conditions above. Mainstream poskim generally treat it as allowed but not ideal, and the "occasional ejaculation" leniency is not the main view.
- **Sephardi and Kabbalah-influenced communities:** The Zohar treats wasting seed as extremely severe. Many Sephardi and Chassidic authorities, influenced by the Zohar and the Arizal, strongly discourage practices that stray from the usual way. Some forbid it outright as a matter of holiness, even though the basic law allows it.

## Limits that always apply
- **Only within marriage.** It is also forbidden during the *niddah* period, when all intimacy is forbidden.
- **Between two men** it is the central act forbidden in [Leviticus 18:22].
- **Health and wellbeing.** Causing harm or pain conflicts with the duty to protect one's body and with the obligation to treat one's spouse with love and dignity.

Practices differ, and the details (consent, the question of seed, a couple's particular situation) matter. A couple with a practical question should ask a rabbi they trust in confidence. Many rabbis and *kallah* and *chatan* teachers (who prepare brides and grooms for marriage) are used to talking about these topics discreetly.

**Usually no, not a separate one.** The Shulchan Arukh does say that someone who slept in his tallit katan should make a bracha on it in the morning. But the Tur and many later authorities disagree. Since we don't say a bracha when it's in doubt, both Ashkenazi and Sephardi practice is the same: when you say the bracha on your tallit gadol in the morning, have in mind that it also covers the tallit katan you're already wearing.

## Key Takeaways
- **Says to bless:** the Mechaber (R. Yosef Karo, author of the Shulchan Arukh), because night isn't the time for tzitzit, so the night breaks the mitzvah [Shulchan Arukh, Orach Chayim 8:16].
- **Says not to bless:** the Tur, Bach, Taz, and the Arizal's practice, because a daytime garment is still obligated at night.
- **Ashkenazim:** the Mishnah Berurah treats it as a doubt and says to cover the tallit katan with the tallit gadol's bracha [Mishnah Berurah 8:42].
- **Sephardim:** the Kaf HaChaim and Ben Ish Chai say not to bless on the tallit katan, and to have it in mind with the tallit gadol.
- **Taking it off:** if you took it off meaning to wait a while before putting it back on, everyone agrees you make a new bracha when you put it on again. But you shouldn't take it off on purpose just to make that happen.

## Where the disagreement comes from
The basic question is whether tzitzit apply at night. The Shulchan Arukh brings two views [Shulchan Arukh, Orach Chayim 18:1]:
- **Rambam:** anything worn at night is exempt.
- **Rosh:** it depends on the garment, not the time. A garment meant for daytime is obligated even when worn at night.

If the Rambam is right, the night interrupted the mitzvah and the morning is a new obligation, so you'd need a bracha. If the Rosh is right, the mitzvah carried on through the night and there's nothing new to bless on.

## The Shulchan Arukh's ruling
The Mechaber writes [Shulchan Arukh, Orach Chayim 8:16]:
> "הלן בטליתו בלילה צריך לברך עליו בבקר אף אם לא פשטו, וטוב למשמש בו בשעת ברכה"
> "One who slept in his tallit at night must bless on it in the morning, even if he did not remove it; and it is good to touch it at the time of the blessing."

The Rema's note on that se'if adds that the same applies to someone who put on his tallit before daybreak.

The Arukh HaShulchan points out that the Tur rules the opposite: the man who slept in his tallit does *not* bless in the morning. He suggests the Mechaber's reasoning is that sleep is a major *hesech hada'at* (break in attention), even under the Rosh's view. He also says the touching is only a nice extra, not required. Still, he concludes that because of the rule *safek berachot lehakel* (when a bracha is in doubt, don't say it), it's best to cover the tallit katan with the tallit gadol [Arukh HaShulchan, Orach Chaim 8:23].

## Ashkenazi practice
The Mishnah Berurah says there's a real dispute, and since a doubtful bracha isn't said, "נכון לכוון לפטור אותה בטלית גדול": it's proper to have in mind that the tallit gadol's bracha covers it [Mishnah Berurah 8:42]. The Chayei Adam rules the same way [Chayyei Adam 12:8].

The Mishnah Berurah adds two practical points:
- **If you took it off** intending not to put it back on right away, you make a new bracha when you put it on, according to everyone. But it isn't proper to plan this just to be able to say a bracha, because according to the view that it isn't needed, that would be an unnecessary bracha.
- **Afternoon nap:** if you take off the tallit katan for a nap, it's unclear whether that counts as a break in attention. So it's better to at least keep it covering you while you sleep. Then nobody would require a bracha when you put it back on.

## Sephardi practice
The Kaf HaChaim reports that the Tur, Bach, Perishah, and Taz all say no bracha [Kaf HaChayim on Shulchan Arukh, Orach Chayim 8:61]. He adds two points:
- The Arizal only made a new bracha when he had taken the garment off to go to the mikveh.
- The Shulchan Arukh's author reportedly changed his mind in a handwritten responsum and said not to bless. The Kaf HaChaim concludes "וכן ראוי לנהוג": this is the right practice.

So Sephardim also follow the advice to cover it with the tallit gadol's bracha. Rav Ovadia Yosef rules the same way in Yalkut Yosef (I'm citing this from memory; I didn't look it up).

The Ben Ish Chai (Parashat Bereishit), as quoted by the Kaf HaChaim, says intention alone is enough and you don't need to touch the tallit katan. Since people forget, he recommends adding these words to the *Leshem Yichud* before putting on the tallit: "והריני מכוין לפטור בברכה זו גם הטלית קטן שעלי" ("and I intend with this bracha to also cover the tallit katan I'm wearing").

## If you don't wear a tallit gadol
This applies, for example, to unmarried men in many Ashkenazi communities. With no tallit gadol, there's no other bracha to cover the tallit katan, and the doubt means you shouldn't bless on it.
- **Common approach:** if you take it off anyway in the morning (to shower or change) and put it back on after a real break, everyone agrees you can then make the bracha.
- **Limit:** the Mishnah Berurah discourages taking it off deliberately just to create that obligation.
- **Chabad:** Chabad follows the Shulchan Aruch HaRav, and its customs here, especially for unmarried men, have their own details. I wasn't able to check that source, so a Chabad user should ask his mashpia or rav.

Consult your rabbi about your own case.

The usual inscription is **"לַה' הָאָרֶץ וּמְלוֹאָהּ"** (*La-Shem ha-aretz u-melo'ah*, "The earth and all it holds belong to God"), written above one's name on the inside cover of a book. A common full form is **"לה' הארץ ומלואה — וספר זה שייך ל[name]"** ("The earth and all it holds are God's, and this book belongs to [name]"). This is a popular custom, not a legal requirement, and people word it in slightly different ways.

## Key Takeaways
- The phrase comes from Psalms 24:1. It says that ultimate ownership belongs to God.
- You write your name under it, so the book is marked as entrusted to you. In Jewish law you still really own it.
- The Talmud reconciles "the earth is God's" with "He gave the earth to people," and that idea sits behind the custom.
- The Lubavitcher Rebbe made this inscription widespread, especially in children's own *sefarim* (holy books).

## The verse
The words open a psalm of David: "לְדָוִד מִזְמוֹר לַה' הָאָרֶץ וּמְלוֹאָהּ תֵּבֵל וְיֹשְׁבֵי בָהּ" ("Of David. A psalm. The earth is God's and all that it holds, the world and its inhabitants") [Psalms 24:1].

## The idea behind it: we own things, but as stewards
The Talmud quotes this verse to teach that enjoying anything in this world without a blessing is like using something consecrated to Heaven [Berakhot 35a]. Rabbi Levi then points out what looks like a contradiction. This verse says the earth is God's, but another verse says "the heavens are the Lord's, and the earth He has given to mankind" (Psalms 115:16). He answers that the first verse describes things *before* a blessing, and the second describes things *after* one.

The inscription holds both sides of that answer:
- **"לה' הארץ ומלואה"** recognizes that everything comes from God.
- **Your name underneath** acknowledges that God has entrusted this book to you, to use and look after properly.

A similar idea appears in Pirkei Avot: "תֶּן לוֹ מִשֶּׁלּוֹ, שֶׁאַתָּה וְשֶׁלְּךָ שֶׁלּוֹ" ("Give Him of what is His, for you and what is yours are His"). The Mishnah supports this with King David's words: "כִּי מִמְּךָ הַכֹּל וּמִיָּדְךָ נָתַנּוּ לָךְ" ("For everything comes from You, and from Your hand we have given to You") [Pirkei Avot 3:7].

One clarification: the inscription is a statement of faith and humility. In practical halacha (Jewish law) a person fully owns their property. They can buy, sell, and lend it, and stealing it is forbidden. "We own nothing" is a spiritual attitude, not a legal rule.

## Who popularized it
- **Chabad:** The Lubavitcher Rebbe urged parents to give even young children their own siddur, Chumash, and tzedakah box. He asked that each be inscribed with "לה' הארץ ומלואה" followed by the child's name. The goal was for children to take pride and responsibility in owning holy books, while knowing from the start that everything really belongs to God. Through this campaign the inscription became common in many communities beyond Chabad.
- **Others:** Many people simply write "שייך ל..." ("belongs to...") or "ספר זה שייך ל..." ("this book belongs to..."). Many also write ב"ה or בס"ד (abbreviations meaning "with God's help") at the top of the page.

## Common wordings
- לה' הארץ ומלואה — [name]
- לה' הארץ ומלואה, וספר זה שייך ל[name]
- בס"ד / ב"ה — ספר זה שייך ל[name]

Any of these is fine. Writing it in a holy book is also a quiet reminder to treat the book respectfully and to say thank you for what you've been given.

The egg is **mourner's food**. The meal right before Tisha B'Av (the *seudah mafseket*, "separating meal") is eaten as if you were a mourner who has just lost a close relative, and a hard-boiled egg is the traditional first food served to a mourner. Its roundness stands for the "wheel" of mourning that turns through the world, and for the mourner who has no "mouth" or opening, meaning he sits in silence. The ashes come from a verse in Eichah (Lamentations), "He has covered me in ashes," and add one more sign of grief for the destroyed Temple.

## Key Takeaways
- The Shulchan Arukh calls eggs (and lentils) *ma'akhalei aveilim*, the foods of mourners.
- The symbolism comes from the Talmud's teaching about the round lentil, which also applies to the egg: mourning circles the world, and the mourner has no "mouth."
- The Rema records the custom of dipping bread in ashes, based on Lamentations 3:16. Many people today dip the egg as well.
- The meal is set up to feel like a mourner's meal "as if his dead lay before him": eaten alone, sitting on the ground, with one simple dish.

## The source in the codes
The Shulchan Arukh writes [Shulchan Arukh, Orach Chayim 552:5]:
> נוהגים לאכול עדשים עם ביצים מבושלים בתוכם שהם מאכלי אבלים
> "We customarily eat lentils with cooked eggs in them, for they are the food of mourners."

Then the Rema adds in his gloss: "ויש נוהגים לאכול ביצים קשים שהוא גם כן מאכל אבלים", "Some have the custom to eat hard-boiled eggs, which are also a food of mourners."

- **Sephardi practice** (Mechaber): lentils with eggs cooked into them.
- **Ashkenazi practice** (Rema): a plain hard-boiled egg. The Mishnah Berurah confirms that this is the custom: "המנהג אצלינו שאוכלים בצים לבד משום אבילות", "our custom is to eat eggs alone, as a sign of mourning" [Mishnah Berurah 552:13].

The same food is served at the *seudat havra'ah*, the first meal neighbors bring to a mourner after the funeral. So on erev Tisha B'Av, each person in effect eats the meal of someone newly bereaved.

## Why an egg? The symbolism
The Talmud (Bava Batra 16b) explains why Yaakov cooked lentils on the day Avraham died. I couldn't pull up that exact passage just now, so I'm paraphrasing what the commentators on the Tur and Shulchan Arukh bring from it:
- **The wheel of mourning.** The lentil is round and rolls, and in the same way mourning rolls through the world and reaches everyone eventually. The egg is round too, so it carries the same message.
- **No mouth.** The lentil has no opening, or "mouth," just as a mourner sits silent and doesn't greet others. A whole egg is closed in the same way.
- Some later writers add a third idea: the egg is a symbol of life and new beginnings. Eating it in grief hints at hope that the cycle will turn again toward redemption. This is a homiletic idea, not part of the halachic source.

## The ashes
The Rema writes [Shulchan Arukh, Orach Chayim 552:6]: "ויש מחמירים לטבל אחר אכילה פת באפר ולאכלו על שם ויגרס בחצץ וגו'", "Some are stringent to dip bread in ashes after eating and eat it, on account of the verse 'He has broken [my teeth] with gravel...'." The full verse is Lamentations 3:16: וַיַּגְרֵס בֶּחָצָץ שִׁנָּי הִכְפִּישַׁנִי בָּאֵפֶר, "He has broken my teeth with gravel; He has covered me in ashes."

The Mishnah Berurah adds that while doing this, one says "זהו סעודת ט"ב", "This is the meal of Tisha B'Av" [Mishnah Berurah 552:16].

Notice that the Rema speaks of dipping **bread** in ashes. The widespread custom of dipping the **egg** grew out of this. It also follows the general way ashes are used in Jewish mourning for Jerusalem, for example the ashes placed on a groom's head.

## The whole meal as a mourner's meal
The Talmud describes the old practice: on erev Tisha B'Av, Rabbi Yehudah bar Ilai was brought dry bread with salt. He sat between the oven and the stove, ate, drank a jug of water, and looked "like one whose dead lay before him" (Taanit 30a–b). The codes follow this:
- Ideally one eats only dry bread with salt and water [Shulchan Arukh, Orach Chayim 552:6].
- The custom is to sit on the ground [Shulchan Arukh, Orach Chayim 552:7].
- The Mishnah Berurah warns not to cut down so much that one can't get through the fast [Mishnah Berurah 552:15]. He also criticizes people who first eat a full cooked meal and only then sit on the floor for the egg. In his view the meal itself has to be the simple mourner's meal [Mishnah Berurah 552:14].

## A related custom: the Seder egg
The Rema also mentions that some eat eggs at the Pesach Seder as a sign of mourning. The reason he gives is that the first night of Pesach always falls on the same night of the week as Tisha B'Av. So even at our happiest table, the egg reminds us of the destruction.

In practice, families differ in how they do these customs: whether they use lentils or a plain egg, whether they dip in ashes, and how strictly they keep the bread-and-water meal. For your own family's custom, ask your rabbi.
